#4937. Ginger Rogers at Home: 10 Photos of the Golden Age Icon’s Glamorous SoCal Life

While most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home. “The little four-room house at 100 Moore Street was the perfect choice” for the future icon’s July 1911 welcome to the world, Rogers concluded in her 1991 memoir, Ginger: My Story. The star would go on to live with her extended family in Kansas City at 3306 Bellefountain Street; with her stepfather in Fort Worth at 1510 Cooper Street; and once she became a Hollywood sensation, a sprawling Beverly Hills estate. That joy and sense of peace she found in her childhood residence became a defining feature of her California pad. “It was a fun house, a happy house,” Rogers told Architectural Digest in 1994. “I was never angry when I didn’t have to work, because I liked to stay home so much.”

Decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the big screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic. Tom Holland will star as Astaire. Read on for a glimpse inside the Oscar winner’s off-set life in the places she cherished most.

After Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together. “I asked Mother if she would like me to build her a house, and if she did, could I live in it with her,” Rogers wrote in her memoir. “The next day she scoured the area for a suitable place to build. She found a wonderful lot high in Beverly Hills on 2.75 acres on Gilcrest Drive in Coldwater Canyon. It had a view that didn’t stop; when the fog burned off late every afternoon, it was possible to see Catalina.” Rogers is pictured at the stunning estate in this 1938 photo.

The actor with her home ice cream fountain.

The Swing Time star added many personal touches to the home, one of which was an elaborate soda fountain. In this 1940 photo, she’s shown whipping up a sweet treat. In her memoir, Rogers recalled all the amenities she installed. “The building took over a year because of labor strikes and material shortages,” she wrote. “When the house was finished, it proved to have been worth waiting for. It had everything I wanted or needed in a house: swimming pool, tennis court, projection room, and my very own soda fountain. Who could ask for anything more?”

Rogers opened her home tennis court to championship hopefuls so they could get practice matches in.

Rogers was an avid tennis player. Though she’s pictured here in 1950 at her Malibu beach house, the actor also had a home court installed at Gilcrest Drive. “On the way to the pool and tennis court were eight sculptured bay leaf trees. Next to the blue-tiled pool was my tennis court. This was my pride and joy,” she wrote in Ginger: My Story. With the knowledge that Rogers had the only en-tout-cas court in the area, the Tennis Association “begged” her to invite young hopefuls for some practice before they went on to championship matches at Forest Hills, New York. “I was delighted to open my court to competitors like Pancho Gonzales, Gussie Moran; and, later, Billie Jean King, Jennifer Hood, and Alice Marble slammed a few over the net too,” Rogers said.

Rogers was known for hosting her Hollywood star friends at home in Beverly Hills.

The Top Hat actor’s Beverly Hills abode was also a hot party spot for Rogers’s A-list friends. “My home was made for entertaining and I gave party after party,” she wrote in her memoir. “Most of them were informal. I’d serve spaghetti and we’d play some night tennis. Alcohol was never served, just cold drinks. One, a mixture of finely crushed ice, 7-Up, and concentrated orange juice, was a real favorite with the tennis crowd.”

The star had a close relationship with her mother, Lela.

Rogers loved living with her mother, with whom she’s pictured in the circa 1940s portrait on the piano in this 1954 image. The triple threat pushed back against the term “stage mother” in Architectural Digest; she considered her mom to be “my guide and my professor… she was my encyclopedia. She knew what route to take: She helped Lucille Ball along hers too, you know. It would have been hard to have a career without her.” About their Beverly Hills pad, she added, “we both liked the look of a French farmhouse. And I wanted certain specific things: a helpful bath, a tennis court, and my own projection room, where we had eight or ten director’s chairs, so that friends could come over to watch movies.”

Rogers with a furry friend at home in the 1950s.

The home featured a main house with bedrooms for Rogers and her mom, as well as a guesthouse for visitors. “The house was very bright,” she told Architectural Digest. “I don’t like dark things; even in my clothing, I prefer to be light and colorful—Springtime for Henry has always been my motto,” she explained, referencing the 1934 comedy. In her memoir, Rogers added, “The style was an American farmhouse with Dutch doors opening to cool breezes. The large bay window in the corner of the living room had a view of Beverly Hills and a bit of Los Angeles. Off the living room was a patio for barbecuing on a flagstone area under a beautiful Australian pepper tree. It was a wonderful place to entertain on crisp California nights.”

Rogers’s home also included a solarium, and bedrooms with scenic views. “On a lower level was an outside entrance to the playroom,” the actor noted in her memoir. “This room had big windows and comfortable cushions as did the solarium in the hallway to the patio. I read many a book, with apple in hand, buried in those downy cushions.” About her bedrooms, she added, “There were two bedrooms leading from the solarium, one for Lelee [her mother] with a four-posted bed and one for me. My room looked out on the view of Beverly Hills, and I had a beautiful hand-carved mantel for my fireplace.”

In addition to the stage talents for which she became a star, Rogers was also a painter. Her guesthouse also doubled as a studio. “My studio, which could double as a guesthouse, held all the paraphernalia of my hobbies: painting materials, canvases, paintbrushes, turpentine, pencils, and so on,” she wrote in her memoir. “Whenever there was a lull on set, I’d take out my pencil and sketch,” Rogers added. “I had been drawing for a long time and it seemed to come naturally to me. I found it challenging and relaxing. I never studied drawing or painting, I just did it.”

In her memoir, Rogers recalled a time when she brought her paintings out for a gallery show. “When I’m not working or traveling, my main source of relaxation comes from my painting,” she wrote. “Gallery owners have wanted to have a one-person show of my work, but I never had the time to organize my paintings. Well, now was the time. Gregg Juarez, a gallery owner and friend of mine, arranged for a show and sale at his gallery in Palm Desert. As we were hanging the paintings for display, I realized these were my children—I couldn’t sell them! Gregg told me I had to sell a few so the customers wouldn’t get mad. I managed to put a few up for sale, but couldn’t part with the rest. So now they are joyously hung in my home for all to see.”

Rogers was 83 years old when she died in 1995 at home in California.

Rogers remained at her home on Gilcrest Drive until 1970, when her mom urged her to sell while she was away working in Europe. “I had been renting it out more than living in it lately, and Mother thought it was financially sound to put it on the market,” the actor wrote in her memoir. “Besides, she said it needed a new roof! She handled all the details of the sale…. This was one time I’m not sure Mother knew best. I adored that house on Gilcrest Drive and have regretted selling it ever since.” Rogers died decades later, on April 25, 1995, at her home in Rancho Mirage, per the Los Angeles Times.

#4936. Tennis is Aces for Healthy Aging

There’s good reason why the United States Tennis Association calls it “the world’s healthiest sport.”

If we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you. But it’s true: Research shows that even recreational tennis can have a seriously impressive impact on your health—now and for years to come.

“Tennis is a whole-body sport,” says sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open. “It offers cardiovascular benefits, muscle strengthening, flexibility—all the things you need to deal with any physical challenges later in life.”

You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr. Colvin adds. In a 2020 study she co-authored, researchers surveyed over 10,000 tennis players, most of them recreational; about 70 percent played just one to three days a week. The players scored higher than the general population on measures such as physical strength, mental and emotional health, and social engagement. “You don't have to be playing at a very high level to get those benefits,” Dr. Colvin says.

And those benefits appear to extend one’s life: When researchers followed 8,577 people for up to 25 years, they found that those who played tennis an average of 103 minutes a week lived 9.7 years longer than their sedentary counterparts. They also lived significantly longer than cyclists (who get an extra 3.7 years), swimmers (3.4 years), and joggers (3.2 years).

Even if you’ve never played tennis before, it’s never too late to start. Keep reading for five reasons to pick up a racket, hit the court, and do your future self a favor.

Tennis involves bursts of high intensity movement—sprinting to the net, running backwards to lob a volley, stopping and then lunging to the opposite side of the court to hit the ball—all of which can do wonders for your cardiovascular health. It boosts heart rate, maximizes your body’s use of oxygen, strengthens heart muscle, improves circulation, and can lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels. As a result, women who play tennis an average two to three hours a week have a 44 percent lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 66 percent lower chance of dying from it.

When you sprint across the court, swing a racquet, or come to a sudden stop, you’re working your leg muscles, core, shoulders, back, and arms—in other words, strengthening nearly every part of the body. A recent study of more than 5,000 women between the ages 63 and 99 found that those who had greater muscle strength lived the longest. And because you’re also supporting your own body weight as you run and land, the sport also helps increase bone density, Dr. Colvin says. Stronger bones mean a lower risk of fractures and osteoporosis in the future, which is what you need if you want to age well.

Tennis requires coordinated movement and muscle control to maintain fluid footwork and smooth, continuous swings. Your core helps make that possible and is key to good balance. Both core strength and balance can help you avoid falls and fractures as you get older. Another part of balance is visuospatial skill—the ability to recognize environmental cues that help you stay upright. Tennis may help sharpen that, too. In a 2022 study, older tennis players who faced a disruption that could throw them off balance were able to react and steady themselves as well as younger players.

Tennis demands intense focus and decision making. “There’s a lot of active thinking going on,” Dr. Colvin says. “You’re making a lot of split-second decisions while you’re playing, plus thinking about the overall strategy of the game. That kind of mental engagement is important as we get older.” According to research, engaging in that kind of quick and strategic thinking while being physically active may be particularly good at promoting neuroplasticity and boosting cognitive function—both of which can stave off the cognitive decline that can come with age.

Studies have found that people who play tennis regularly tend to be less stressed or anxious than people who do lower-intensity exercise. They also report feeling more optimistic, less depressed, and a greater sense of well-being. Like other high-energy sports, tennis may boost mood by prompting the release of brain chemicals such as endorphins, dopamine, and serotonin. It’s also a fun game to play with friends. “The social aspect of tennis is one of its key benefits,” Dr. Colvin says. Numerous studies show that those kinds of community ties are essential for a long, healthy, happier life. With tennis, that’s built into the game.

#4935. When We Forgive, What New Meaning Do We Find in Life?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills

Suffering could lead to despair, depression, hopelessness, and even not liking oneself (Yu et al. 2021; Reed & Enright, 2006). Yet one aspect of the forgiveness process, especially as one nears the end of the forgiveness journey, is the sometimes surprising development of finding meaning in that suffering and a new purpose in life. Finding meaning centers on an important question: What have I learned from going through this suffering, and what have I learned as I walked the journey of forgiveness? This is a cognitive exercise that can lead to new short-term and long-term goals (Enright, 2015). In other words, the cognitive exercise of finding meaning can lead to behaviors that support new purposes in one’s life.

The psychotherapist and Holocaust survivor, Viktor Frankl (1969/2014), pioneered this idea of finding meaning in suffering as he endured the persecution of his imprisonment. His motivation was to resist being destroyed by the abuse. By finding meaning, one can transcend suffering and make it more bearable.

When I discuss the theme of finding meaning in suffering through forgiveness, I am not focusing on the injustice but on its aftermath. The basic question is this: What are you learning about life as you extend mercy to those who were deeply unfair to you? This post explores the different meanings people tend to generate as they forgive.

Let us first start by examining what finding meaning in suffering is not, because it can be misunderstood.

Consider three themes that sometimes are confused with finding meaning in what an unjustly acting person has done to the forgiver.

First, the forgiver is not denying the disappointment, sadness, anger, or grief in what was suffered. The injustice did happen, and the negative response is real. In other words, finding meaning is not some kind of non-feeling, interpreted, at least temporarily, as relief from the effects of the injustice.

Second, the person does not play games with themselves, stating, for example, “Oh well, things happen for a reason, and I’ll just make the best of it by accepting it.” Yes, people can “make the best of it,” but if this is an exclusive meaning of suffering, the one who forgives is not going after the woundedness inside, which may linger for a long time. The “oh well” approach is passive. To heal from the effects of the injustice, a person needs a more active approach to the pain.

Third, the forgiver does not distort reality by thinking, “Well, all things happen for good reasons, and so I will try to see the good in what happened to me.” The injustice was not good. Some aspects of what happens after the injustice may be good, but the injustice itself is not.

1. Being more sensitive to the suffering of others, even those who never hurt you: James, upon forgiving, realized he had what he called a “short temper,” in which he imposed his anger on unsuspecting others. He has now committed, for example, to being more patient and kind to cashiers in grocery stores and pharmacies as he waits in line. He is more sensitive to the fatigue and stress of those working behind the cash register. This gives him a new sense of purpose, as he recognizes his intemperance in these contexts and now works to overcome his anger.

2. Being motivated to help others in their suffering: When Dr. Freedman (Freedman & Enright, 1996) worked with female incest survivors on a long-term forgiveness intervention, she saw that many of them, upon forgiving, became motivated to help other incest survivors overcome their deep resentment. They were not choosing as a goal to become mental health professionals, but instead to be of assistance to others who have suffered as they have.

As another example, I talked with a man who is imprisoned for life. Upon forgiving those who abused him, he said to me that he knows he will never get out of the correctional institution, but now he is motivated to help his cellmates forgive and to be unburdened of their anger. This led to a new purpose, or the behavioral manifestation of this desire to assist others.

3. Standing in the pain so you do not throw that pain onto others: The paradox of standing in the pain is this: As people bear the negative effects of unjust treatment by not throwing that pain back to the offending person or to unsuspecting others, the pain-bearers realize they are stronger than they thought. They see the positive outcomes of not seeking revenge. As Gandhi said, if we keep taking an eye for an eye, the whole world will be blind. The pain-bearers realize they can now translate this into a new purpose of contributing to a more peaceful world.

4. Forgiving helps us think more deeply about justice: If people are continually treated unjustly, they can find meaning in living a life of mercy and fairness integrated together. Thus, their understanding of justice can become wiser, and therefore their appropriation of justice can become more helpful to others.

5. Eventually, you can develop an overall philosophy of life, such as committing to be a conduit of good in this world: This is what Dr. Frankl called supra-meaning, or a new philosophy of life that encompasses an overall approach to how one interacts with others and why one does so in this way. For example, a person can commit to living a life of greater respect, kindness, and love toward both offenders and others. For example, Sally decided to resist impatience and negative emotions toward her own children, as a way of life in her family, so that these life-giving moral virtues can become norms there.

6. As people find meaning in their suffering, they can put their future purpose in life into sharper perspective: Finding meaning, in other words, becomes the cognitive rationale and emotional motivation to seek what matters to them.

In summary, our suffering is not for nothing. People who suffer and forgive can develop as they think carefully about what they are learning about suffering, their own humanity, and life itself. As Dr. Frankl learned and passed his wisdom on to us, finding meaning in suffering opens unexpected doors for survival and growing in our humanity.

Enright, R.D. (2015). 8 keys to forgiveness. Norton.

Frankl, V. (1969/2014). The will to meaning: Foundations and applications of logotherapy. Plume.

Freedman, S. R., & Enright, R. D. (1996). Forgiveness as an intervention goal with incest survivors. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 64(5), 983-992.

Reed, G. & Enright, R.D. (2006). The effects of forgiveness therapy on depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress for women after spousal emotional abuse. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 74, 920-929.

Yu, L., Gambaro, M., Song, J., Teslik, M., Komoski, M.C., Wollner, B., & Enright, R.D. (2021). Forgiveness therapy in a maximum-security correctional institution: A randomized clinical trial. Clinical Psychology and Psychotherapy, 28, 1457-1471.

#4933. Beef Prices Are at Record Highs—But There’s a Smart Way You Can Save Cash and Score Quality Meat

Editor’s Note: When I originally reported this article in 2014, a pound of ground beef cost roughly $3.50. Now that same amount of protein costs you $6.75. But nothing about buying beef wholesale has changed: You will still save more money over time if you purchase an eighth, a quarter, a half, or even a whole cow given you have the upfront cash and deep freezer space to store it all. (A quarter of a cow from the same farm I purchased mine now costs $1,100, in case you were wondering.)

And, if you can spring for grass-fed beef, there’s been more recent published research to show that it might be healthier for you than the grain-fed variety. In 2022, South Korean researchers found that grass-fed beef contained a healthier fatty acid profile than grain-fed beef. Same goes for a 2026 study published in the Journal of Animal Science.

While eating healthier is great, doing so has to taste amazing too. Luckily that hasn’t changed about grass-fed beef either.

THE COW I ate was born in rural Pennsylvania. Cathy Pomanti, the owner of Sugar Hill Farm, midwifed my calf into the world. Pomanti raises grass-fed organic Scottish Highland Cows, a shaggy breed yielding meat that’s among the tastiest on the planet. On one farm visit, my fiancee saw a highlander, went quiet, and then said, “I don’t want to eat them. I want to hug them.” But I was hungry for a cow to call my own.

As a pleasure-seeking meat eater, disappointed by grain-fed supermarket beef. Rib eyes require a slick of steak sauce to taste meaty. Ground beef has a tacky, greasy consistency. Tenderloin, even with tender care, always leaves me underwhelmed. So I decided to stop complaining about mass-market beef and find a rancher. I wanted to know my cattle producer. I wanted to know my cow.

My cow never had a name; Pomanti can’t bring herself to name cows headed for slaughter. But he did have a good life. My cow spent his first 10 months growing strong on his mother’s milk, sticking close by her side. Then Pomanti separated my cow and his mother into different pens. My cow bawled. His mother mooed. It was for the best. Once Mom stopped producing milk, the two were reunited, but my cow now preferred delicious, nutritious grass.

Over the next year and a half, my cow grew an impressive coat of thick, coarse hair. Because he wouldn’t be subjected to the diseases and indignities of the industrial feedlot, he didn’t need antibiotics or growth hormones. Those substances wouldn’t end up in me or my fiancée, either.

Last October, my cow was loaded onto a truck and taken to Rising Spring Meat Company, an organic butcher outside State College, Pennsylvania. There he was held in a pen, calm and comfortable, until he was humanely shot in the head. The carcass was then halved and hung in a cooler to dry-age, a process that helps tenderize the meat, for about 14 days. Next my cow was cut into pieces, vacuum-sealed, and delivered to Pomanti.

She summoned me for the handoff. Out of her massive freezer units she pulled bags bursting with marrow bones, globular ground beef portions, and a tenderloin the size of Popeye’s forearm. I drove the box of beef back home that day, dreaming of meals to come, under a sky with clouds that looked like heifers.

AS A TYPICAL American, you ate a hefty 51 pounds of beef last year, the USDA says. That’s roughly the equivalent of 65 T-bones or 204 quarter-pound burger patties.

The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association notes that less than 1 percent of beef sold at retail is labeled as grass-fed. During the “finishing,” the animal begins to lay down more fat in relation to muscle and bone growth, says Cindy Daley, Ph.D., who studies beef at California State University.

Until the 1950s, ranchers finished cattle exclusively on grass. But industrial producers realized that grain feeding improved fat marbling while cutting the days until slaughter. After decades of eating the stuff, we now prefer fattier beef. But at the same time, our rates of diseases linked to inflammation rose.

Could grain-fed cows and inflammation be connected? A 2011 Irish study found that people who replaced their regular red meat with three weekly servings of grass-fed red meat for a month improved their inflammation-fighting omega-3 fatty acid profiles by 37 percent over those of people who ate the same amount of grain-finished red meat.

Though the diet studies are too small to be conclusive, a 2010 research review led by Daley found that grass-fed beef outclassed grain-fed nutritionally, with triple the immune-boosting vitamin E, up to five times the heart-healthy omega-3 fatty acids, and seven times the antioxidant carotenoids.

If grass-fed beef was going to treat me better, I needed to return the favor. So I began contacting chefs. The recipes that follow taught me key kitchen skills, but they also taught me something deeper: If you know your beef, you love it even more.

THERE’S A CERTAIN comfort in dissociating yourself from the animal you’re eating for dinner. If you don’t think about where on the cow’s body the meat comes from, you don’t have to contemplate the death and dismemberment involved in its trip to your plate. The oxtail, however, made a very specific statement about its origins. It came to me in three pieces, which, because of my morbid curios- ity, I arranged to reconstruct the entire appendage. I imagined my cow using it to swat flies. It wasn’t simply a meal. It was a sacrifice.

Alice Waters, executive chef of Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California, and founder of the Edible Schoolyard Project, recommends cooking oxtail in a classic braise. “With grain-fed beef, you’re tasting a richness and tenderness, but it’s not the real flavor,” Waters says. “It’s like cooking vegetables with a lot of butter: You can’t taste the vegetables.” Her technique, inspired by a recipe from Zuni Café in San Francisco, matches the beautiful beefiness of the rustic cut while also turning it fork-tender.

Bonus: You can apply the same braising technique to other tough bone-in cuts your purveyor may pass along, such as shanks or short ribs.

2 lb grass-fed oxtails1 Tbsp Kosher salt4 cups beef stock2 Tbsp olive oil1 ¾ cups red wine2 bay leaves1 small head garlic, halved crosswise1 sprig thyme3 black peppercorns1 large carrot, peeled and roughly chopped3 celery stalks, roughly chopped1 medium yellow onion, quartered1 cup drained canned tomatoes, roughly chopped

1. For the best flavor, salt the oxtails two days before cooking.

2. Trim the oxtails of excess fat. In a medium saucepan, cook the stock over medium heat until reduced by half, about 30 minutes.

3. In a skillet, heat the oil on medium. Pat the oxtails dry and brown them, 3 to 4 minutes. Set aside. Wipe the skillet, add the wine, stir, and cook it down by half, about 5 minutes. Add the stock.

4. Preheat the oven to 300°F. In a roasting pan, add the remaining ingredients; add stock to cover by a third. Simmer on medium low. Cover.

5. Place the pan in the oven and cook 3 to 4 hours. Then crack the lid and cook until the meat is very tender, another 20 to 30 minutes. Serve oxtails with sauce. Makes 8 servings

I NEEDED TO do something special with the most prestigious cut of my cow: the 14-pound standing rib roast. The meal should be special but also very simple, says Donald Link, owner and executive chef of Cochon and Butcher in New Orleans. Anything too fussy would only detract from its intense, glorious beefiness.

For maximum flavor, you want to cook this behemoth roast only to medium rare, Link told me. Because the cut is so large, the preparation and resting stages are critical. If the meat is too cold before it enters the oven, it’ll be raw in the center when it exits. If you carve into it immediately after cooking, you’ll lose a reservoir of delicious juices. Patience is paramount.

And the rewards are well worth the wait: “Good grass-fed beef tastes cleaner. You don’t have that heavy feeling in your gut after you eat it,” Link says. I heard similar accolades from the friends and family members I invited over to dinner. In fact, most people said the steaks, liver, or carne asada I’d served them tasted “like beefier beef” and “less greasy.” One guest who tasted the rib roast said she woke up the morning after our dinner fantasizing about the beef from the night before.

1 grass-fed beef rib roast (14 lb)Olive oil

1. To promote even doneness, remove the roast from the refrigerator 2 hours before cooking.

2. Place the roast on a wire rack set on a baking sheet. The last 30 minutes prior to cooking, place a fan in front of the meat to dry excess moisture and foster caramelization.

3. Preheat the oven to 450°F. Lightly rub the roast on all sides with olive oil and then liberally coat it with salt and freshly ground pepper. Set it back on the wire rack atop the baking sheet and place it in the oven.

4. Cook until well browned on the outside, about 20 minutes. Lower the heat to 275°F and continue to cook until a digital thermometer inserted into the center of the roast reads 140°F, about 2 hours. Remove the roast and let it rest until it’s almost at room temperature, about 45 minutes.

5. Serve with roasted potatoes and a simple salad. Makes 20 to 25 servings

OF THE 51 pounds of cow you ate last year, about half was ground. Here’s a scary fact: U.S. ground beef is not easily traced and may not even be from the United States, a 2013 review in Meat Science reveals. All the more reason to buddy up to a rancher.

You can make a grass-fed beef burger (I did), but you’d be depriving your tastebuds if you didn’t venture beyond familiar ground. “Grass-fed beef is very lean by nature. Grinding beef for burgers involves adding fat, and if you’re using grass-fed, you lose something,” says Sang Yoon, executive chef of Father’s Office and Lukshon in L.A. That something, he says, is the herbaceous flavor imparted by the cow’s diet. Make larb instead, Yoon says. This Southeast Asian dish packs a barrage of fresh herbs to flatter grass-fed beef.

1 Tbsp uncooked jasmine rice6 Tbsp peanut oil12 oz grass-fed ground beef1 shallot, minced2 garlic cloves, sliced2 fresh Thai chiles, thinly sliced1 Tbsp palm sugar2 Tbsp fish sauce¼ cup lime juice1 head cabbage, leaves separated½ cilantro leaves½ mint leaves½ Thai basil leaves4 scallions, sliced

1. In a small pan on medium heat, toast the rice, stirring often. Cool and grind the rice to a fine powder in a clean coffee or spice grinder.

2. In a wok or big cast-iron skillet, heat the oil on medium high until it shimmers. Add the beef; cook, stirring occasionally, until it begins to brown, 2 to 3 minutes. Add the shallot, garlic, chiles, palm sugar, and fish sauce.

3. Remove from the heat and add the lime juice and rice powder. Stir well and season with salt.

4. Let the mixture cool slightly before serving. Spoon the mixture into individual cabbage cups and garnish with herbs and scallions. Makes 6 to 8 servings

MARC FORGIONE, OWNER and executive chef of Restaurant Marc Forgione in New York City, told me I should start by not cooking the beef at all. “The best way to experience grass-fed beef, because it’s so lean, is to eat it raw,” says Forgione.

When I asked him if it was dangerous to eat DIY steak tartare, Forgione told me that as long as the beef is high in quality and its temperature never rises above 40°F for longer than 40 minutes, your risk of illness will be very low, he says. And Pomanti, for her part, says bacterial contamination among her cattle is vir- tually nonexistent. (It pays to know your source.)

So I sharpened my knives for a rare opportunity. The result was a luscious tartare that topped variations I’ve tasted at the country’s top steakhouses.

1 Tbsp minced onion1 Tbsp minced cornichons1 tsp minced parsley2 anchovies, minced½ Tbsp Dijon mustard2 or 3 dashes Tabasco sauce2 tsp Worcestershire sauce½ cup, plus 2 Tbsp olive oil1 lb grass-fed beef tenderloinWarm toast

1. In a small bowl, mix the onion, parsley, cornichons, and anchovies. Reserve.

2. In a blender or food processor, add the mustard, Tabasco, Worcestershire, and 2 Tbsp olive oil. Puree, gradually adding the remaining olive oil until emulsified. Reserve.

3. Place the tenderloin in the freezer for about 5 minutes for easier cutting. Then, working quickly, slice it into ¼-inch-thick pieces.

4. In a medium serving bowl, combine the meat with the reserved ingredients. Season with salt and pepper to taste. Mix well.

5. Chill in the fridge for 10 minutes before serving atop warm toast. Makes 8 servings as an appetizer

WHEN MY TOUR of the special cuts was complete, I dug for the last of the T-bones that were stashed aside the cow’s heart (yes, the heart) in the freezer. Steaks were the first cuts I cooked, and I still craved them. Naomi Pomeroy, the executive chef of Beast in Portland, Oregon, had taught me to sear them to a juicy medium rare. She’s a pro; she cooks grass-fed beef exclusively.

I preheated my oven to 350°F and placed a cast-iron skillet over medium heat. I cranked some freshly ground black pepper and scattered kosher salt over each side of the steak. Then I added a good knob of butter to the skillet, allowed it to melt, and followed it with the steak and a few sprigs of parsley and thyme. I listened for the sizzling to subside, awaiting the aroma of a baseball field on a hot summer day. Those signs told me it was time to flip the meat and then slide it into the oven, skillet and all. There it basked for five minutes until the interior temperature reached 122°F. Out of the oven it came. I then basted it reverently with the rest of the melted butter, tented some aluminum foil over the skillet, and let it rest for what seemed like an eternity. Okay, five minutes. And then I savored every last juicy, earthy, hearty, powerful, tender bite. The celebration of my cow was complete.

Yes, grass-fed beef costs more money than the grain-finished variety, but you’re making that investment to enjoy superior meat that is less fatty, more nutrient-dense, better for your body, and certainly better on the palate.

And if you purchase your grass-fed beef in bulk, so much the better. It can be less expensive than grass-fed cuts you’d find in the store, for one thing. There’s also something deeply comfort- ing about possessing a large amount of premium meat. (Zombie apocalypse be damned!) But because you know the life of your cow, and the rancher who raised that animal, you also want to honor that cow in death. It’s not just dinner. It’s your duty.

This shoe was also crowned the best overall Brooks walking shoe by our associate style editor, Shannon Zitz. “The firm-yet-cozy midsole hugs the foot just right, offering a secure, locked-in feel that still stays comfortable mile after mile,” she says. Your friend is sure to love it, too (and if “shopping for a friend” is code for buying yourself a pair, we totally get it!)Read more: Best Brooks Walking Shoes

Sweat-proof, waterproof, and featherweight, these wireless headphones for working out are a runner’s dream. “These allow me to hear oncoming traffic, people, and other outside noise with their wrap-around, open-ear design while delivering feel-good jams,” says Accardi, who loves using them on her runs.

Help a fitness friend stay comfortable and chic as the months get colder with this soft, sweat-wicking jacket from Lululemon. It has a flattering fit that looks good on everyone, and works when paired with leggings, running shorts, and even joggers. I own at least three different versions of this cult-favorite, and it’s guaranteed to be a slam-dunk gift.

There’s a lot for a giftee to love about the Vuori Classic Energy T-shirt. First, the fabric is soft, light, and wicking while at the same time not screaming “technical fabric,” so this top can go straight from daily life to the gym. It would also be perfect for a travel capsule wardrobe for just about any scenario. The second is the fit, which is drapey, modern, and super comfortable. Add to all this that it comes in a wide range of colors, and this may be one of the most versatile T-shirts ever.

Everyone loves choices. This insulated water bottle easily switches between a straw and a chug opening, so your friend will be able to sip—or gulp—their water, depending on their preference in the moment. It’s also leakproof (we tested), so that refreshing bottle of water won’t leak all over everything if they throw it in their gym bag. Plus, there are 10 different colors to choose from, so it’ll match your friends’ style, too.

A high-quality percussion massage gun is really a must-have for anyone who trains IMHO. And this popular recovery tool makes for a great gift for everyone else who wants to take care of tight muscles. The Hypervolt Pro 3 is one that we love. In fact, we named it the best overall in our massage gun buyer’s guide. It’s a can’t-go-wrong gift for the active people in your life.

I’m low-key obsessed with this gym bag, which I’ve been testing for over a month. It’s perfect for the friend who needs a gym bag that keeps her (tons of) stuff well-organized while also looking stylish. While it’s technically a well-designed gym bag, the Vuori Gym Bag 2.0 is really a multitasker that can do more than schlep sweaty workout gear. This bag’s 39L capacity, zippered shoe compartment, and interior pockets (even including a lined wet pocket) mean it can easily do double duty as both well-organized gym bag and weekend getaway bag. Who doesn’t love gear that can check multiple boxes?

The Outwork has been a favorite shoe among WH editors who love to lift for quite a while, thanks to its low 4mm drop, bombproof durability, wide toe box that allows to foot to splay, and a solid, stable outsole—all essential components to an ideal weightlifting shoe (because nobody should be lifting in squishy sneakers or running shoes). These shoes won a WH Fitness Award, we love them so much. And with over forty (yes, forty!) colors to chose from, you’ll be able to find the pair that matches your giftee’s style perfectly.

Therabody is a leader in the recovery space, and massage guns and compression boots from the brand are among our faves. But you can’t use a massage gun in more delicate areas of the body so many of us often feel tight and sore, such as the neck and jaw. So when I heard about this facial massager designed specifically for that purpose, I knew I had to test it. It didn’t disappoint, and I found tender spots at the base of my skull that I didn’t even know I had, and the tech neck tension at the end of the day has met its match. Your giftee will be able to learn exactly how to use this little guy to get the same relief, thanks to the Therabody app that includes guided demos and routines.

With so many people embracing everything analog, give the gift of less screen time in the form of a dedicated workout journal designed to make it easy to track progress and stay motivated. This well-designed workout journal offers structured pages to log exercises, sets, reps, goals, and nutrition. Compact and sleek, it can easily be tossed in a gym bag and become a physical record of fitness goals accomplished.

It’s no secret that WH editors are obsessed with Lululemon leggings. They’re awesome for any workout—HIIT, running, yoga, boxing, you name it—with their buttery-soft fabric, weightless fit, and high-rise waistband. Our favorite? The Align No Line leggings, which are an upgrade from the OG without seams at the front for added comfort. They’re also functional for recovery days, relaxing at home, or running errands around town. They come in loads of different colors to match any friends’ taste.

A weighted vest is perfect for adding resistance to simple movements like walking and squatting. This WH Fitness Award winner has a cross-style fit specifically designed for a woman’s body, offering support across the shoulder blades. “It elevates my walks, helps my core activate more, and makes my bodyweight exercises harder,” says WH associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian. The straps are adjustable, as is the weight. The 10-pound model can go as low as four pounds (when you remove weights), so your friend can keep progressing as they get stronger.

Wearing a fitness tracker reminds me of the adage, “what gets measured gets done.” And when what’s getting done is improving health and fitness, a fitness tracker can be seriously motivating. A Whoop fitness tracker is the perfect gift for that person who’s ready to understand their body better and level up their fitness. With detailed insights into recovery, sleep, HRV, stress levels, and more displayed and tracked over time in an intuitive-to-use app, this standard-setting fitness tracker will help your fitness-obsessed friend understand their body better, optimize their training, and lock in.

If you search “Jennifer Aniston workout” on the internet, the result it spits out will be Pvolve, the functional training system she has reportedly been a devotee of since 2021. Often described as “pilates inspired,” the system is especially effective for building core and back strength. While there are several bundles to chose from, it’s hard to beat the workout you can get from this Pvolve travel set while camping out in a relative’s guest room during the holidays. It’s not just for travel, though. It’s also great for a functional workout while staying put, considering the tiny footprint of all the equipment (it fits in a drawer). The accompanying app has guided workouts and everything else your giftee needs to know.

If your friend lives at barre classes, snag them a few pairs of these non-slip socks. Machine-washable and grippy, these socks come in a variety of cute colors, including mulberry and sky blue. Isabel McMahon, WH’s assistant social media editor, loves that they have crisscross straps to help keep a snug fit during yoga and Pilates classes. “I wouldn’t mind finding a few more in my stocking this year!” she said.

Raise your hand if your upper back feels tight after a long day. (Raises hand.) Chances are good that your giftee’s hand would be up right now, too. Lying on this wheel and taking deep breathes is one of my favorite ways to unlock and stretch my upper back. It’s a tool that’s as simple to use as it is effective so a sometimes hard to mobilize area of the body. I’ve actually gifted this to several people myself to both “fitness people” and older relatives.

Few shoe brands have a grip on the running community like Hoka, which is known for highly cushioned footwear with a distinctive rocker shape. The latest editor-fave from the brand, the Clifton 11, is squishy and flexible, with impressive traction to keep your favorite runner on their feet. After testing just about every Hoka model out there, WH associate style editor Shannon Zitz ranked the Clifton 11 as the best overall Hoka walking shoe. “It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning that gives me a spring in my step,” she says. They’ll be sure to convert to a Hoka stan.

The Bose Ultra Open Wireless Earbuds gently hug your ears to stay securely in place, making them a great choice for nearly any type of workout. They’re a great alternative for people who lost their AirPods one time too many or don’t like the feeling of wrap-around headphones like Shokz. Plus, the open format means being able to maintain awareness of the surroundings while listening. The seven-hour battery life is handy, too.

#4931. Why the Word “Boundaries” Makes Boomer Parents Mad

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods

When the topic of boundaries comes up, a Millennial woman (born 1981-1996 according to Pew Research) will vigorously nod in agreement. But when that same daughter tries to install those boundaries with her Baby Boomer mother, (born between 1946-1964, according to Pew Research), the reaction can be swift and negative: Mom gives a raised eyebrow, a long silence, or an extreme and snarky reply.

How did a word meant to build healthier relationships become one that is so triggering? Why do boundaries make your family members feel rejected? The issue isn't the new behavior and delineation itself, but what the word signals.

For some adult daughters (Gen X were born 1965-1980; Millennials born 1981-1996; and even adult Gen Z (born 1997-2012, according to Pew Research), boundaries represent a way to honor yourself, not give up on the elements in a relationship that matter to you, and hopefully reflect your evolving emotional maturity. For a Baby Boomer parent, boundary talk sounds like withdrawal, rejection, and pulling away from the family (or particularly from them).

Part of the problem is that the paradigm of “Boomers vs. Millennials” has become a ready-made cultural storyline. In a 2026 study of Instagram memes about the two generations, media researchers Centorrino and Ferrigno found that the largest group of memes did one thing above all: draw lines between generations. That is, sow division between the Millennial and the Boomer. These memes ranged from dismissive jokes like “OK Boomer” to side-by-side comparisons of what each generation was like at the same age, but with a negative twist. The researchers argue that generational labels work less like neutral categories and more like symbolic boundaries, sorting people into “us” and “them.” It can become a crass classification system or a way of saying "they're not like me and my peers."

With this culturally sensitive division in mind, when a daughter deploys the language of boundaries, her mother may not hear a healthy limit. She may hear one more line being drawn between “your generation” and “mine.” In short, she feels pushed away and made fun of for her behaviors and ways of doing things. That's a pretty big barrier to hearing their adult child in a neutral or healthy way.

Research on adult development helps explain why this mismatch runs so deep. Karen Fingerman, a leading researcher on parents and adult children, and her colleagues draw on socioemotional selectivity theory. This theory suggests that as people age, they become more invested in keeping their longest-standing close ties than in forming new ones. That means they get really zoned-in on their adult children, their own siblings, and lifelong close friends.

In a 2024 study of more than 300 adults aged 65 and older, Fingerman’s team found that nearly three-quarters of participants’ long-term relationships were with family. That means most of what an older person wants is from their adult kids. They're invested in these long-term relationships with a deep intensity. However, the parent-child ties were also complicated. The time older folks spent with their family members was linked to more stressful conversations and intense moods (both positive and negative). All this means that Boomer parents are putting an intense lens on their adult child and it's kind of stressful.

And here's the rub. That intensity only goes one way. Researchers have described the concept of “intergenerational stake”: parents tend to be more invested in their children than children are in their parents. In a 2015 study of more than 600 middle-aged adults, Kira Birditt, Fingerman, and colleagues found that people rated their relationships with their children as both more important and more negative than their relationships with their own parents. Friction, in other words, can be a sign of how much a relationship matters. In sum, the more an adult child matters to their parent, the more likely there's tension as they seek connection.

Why does that friction occur? Fingerman’s earlier work points to an answer. In a 1996 study of 48 mothers over 70 and their middle-aged daughters, she introduced the term “developmental schism” to describe tension that arises because mothers and daughters are at different points in adult development. That's the sandpaper feeling between mothers and adult daughters, even when there's a lot of love. Two of the biggest sources of that tension were independence and how much importance each person places on the relationship. Many of today’s Boomer mothers were once the daughters in research like this, navigating the same tug-of-war with their own mothers. They haven't forgotten that. They're trying to discern how to manage things well with their own daughters, but sometimes it still comes off poorly.

That is the boundary conversation in a nutshell. A daughter may be focused on protecting her time, energy, and independence. Her mother is at a stage of life when she is intensely focused on family ties. She's laser-focused on keeping the relationship close, but maybe doesn't have the skills to make it happen, just the desire for it to be so. Both daughter and mother are responding to real needs. They just aren’t the same needs.

And nowhere does that mismatch become more visible than during the holidays, when traditions, expectations, and family identities are on full display.

As a family communication researcher, I’ve spent more than a decade studying the invisible work of daughtering: the task, emotional, cognitive, and identity labor adult daughters do to keep families connected. Lately, I’ve become especially interested in what happens when daughters begin to renegotiate that work.

Boundary conflict isn’t really about what a daughter is willing to do or a wall she's putting in place with her mother. The tension is about what these boundaries end up meaning to everyone else. A daughter's work (or lack thereof) ripples to every corner of the family. When she decides to prioritize some needs more than others and set down some of the unnecessary labor she's been doing, expect the family to shift, either seismically or gently, but it will change nonetheless. But you should know, daughter, you have every right not to abandon yourself and your needs. Set the boundary, but don't be shocked when others dislike it or feel hurt. Wait it out with empathy and gentle understanding. A new paradigm is on the horizon.

Centorrino, M., & Ferrigno, C. (2026). Memetic narratives of generational conflict: The “boomers vs. millennials” frame on Instagram. Journalism and Media, 7(3), 187. https://www.mdpi.com/2673-5172/7/3/187

Birditt, K. S., Hartnett, C. S., Fingerman, K. L., Zarit, S., & Antonucci, T. C. (2015). Extending the intergenerational stake hypothesis: Evidence of an intraindividual stake and implications for well-being. Journal of Marriage and Family, 77(4), 877–888. https://doi.org/10.1111/jomf.12203

Fingerman, K. L. (1996). Sources of tension in the aging mother and adult daughter relationship. Psychology and Aging, 11(4), 591–606. https://doi.org/10.1037/0882-7974.11.4.591

Fingerman, K. L., Zhou, Z., Huo, M., Luong, G., & Birditt, K. S. (2024). Enduring bonds: Duration and contact in close relationships in late life. The Gerontologist, 64(4), gnad091. https://doi.org/10.1093/geront/gnad091
